articles.title: Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez calls snap election
articles.description: The Spanish prime minister had repeatedly insisted he would serve out his four-year term, with elections scheduled for 2027.
articles.body:
The Spanish prime minister had repeatedly insisted he would serve out his four-year term, with elections scheduled for 2027.
https://p.dw.com/p/5Nkio Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez speaks at a news conference in Madrid (FILE 11/11/2024) Image: Burak Akbulut/Anadolu/picture alliance Advertisement Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez called an early general election on Monday, bringing forward a vote that had been scheduled for 2027.
Sanchez announced the decision in a statement at Madrid's Moncloa Palace after a weekend of consultations with his closest advisers.
"It is time for Spaniards to decide what future you want," Sanchez said.
The announcement of the November 29 vote follows a parliamentary defeat for his minority government on Friday , when lawmakers rejected measures aimed at tackling Spain's housing crisis.
Sanchez framed the election as a choice over Spain's future direction, saying voters must decide whether the country joins what he called a "far-right wave" or continues on a path of "openness, social justice and environmental responsibility."
He said he trusted Spanish voters to make that choice.
"To do more, we need to renew and broaden the support of the people," Sanchez said, adding that his aim was "to secure a much broader, progressive majority in parliament."
The decision comes despite Sanchez repeatedly insisting in recent months that his government would complete its four-year term.
The election follows mounting public pressure over housing costs, with large protests across the country.
Tens of thousands of people marched in Madrid and other Spanish cities on Saturday to demand more affordable housing.
Opposition parties on Friday rejected government measures that included automatically extending tenancy contracts and restricting the eviction of vulnerable tenants.
The parliamentary defeat highlighted the difficulties Sanchez's minority coalition has faced in passing legislation. Spain has also been operating for several years under its 2023 budget, the last national spending plan approved under Sanchez.
Housing protests intensified after the eviction last month of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal from the Madrid apartment where she had lived for decades. Hundreds of protesters have since set up a tent camp in central Madrid.
Recent opinion polls have generally put the opposition conservative Popular Party ahead of Sanchez's Socialist Workers' Party.

articles.title: Spain: Massive protests after housing bills voted down
articles.description: Organizers estimated that 500,000 people turned out in the streets of Madrid to demand affordable housing. Similar protests were held in around 50 other Spanish cities.
articles.body:
Organizers estimated that 500,000 people turned out in the streets of Madrid to demand affordable housing. Similar protests were held in around 50 other Spanish cities.
https://p.dw.com/p/5NhwC The latest wave of protests emerged in response to the forced eviction of an elderly woman in Madrid Image: Alejandro Martinez Velez/REUTERS Advertisement Tens of thousands of people protested across Spain on Saturday to demand affordable housing .
The protests come a day after the Spanish parliament narrowly voted down two emergency bills designed to support renters and prevent evictions.
"It only proves that it is us the people who have to adapt ‌to the political parties, and not the politicians to ‌what ​the people want, and this can't go on like that," one 26-year-old protester in Madrid told the Reuters news agency.
They are the latest demonstrations in a week-long wave of actions that began in response to the eviction of an 87-year-old woman, Maricarmen Abascalin , in Madrid.
"What we are feeling in the streets is a new energy that we haven't seen in a long time, and energy that is showing that eight days of people's power can achieve more than eight years of progressive government," said Valeria Racu, one of the spokespeople of the Tenants' Union organizing Saturday's protest.
Police said around 70,000 people took part in the demonstration in Madrid. Organizers put the figure closer to 500,000 people.
Additional protests were held in around 50 other cities.
In the eastern city of Valencia, police used tear gas and rubber bullets against protesters.
Dozens of protesters had managed to get inside Valencia's City of Arts and Sciences — a major landmark in the city — before they were ejected by police.
Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez's proposed emergency measures included automatic renewal of tenancy contracts and restrictions on evicting vulnerable tenants. However, bills were shot down by opposition parties on Friday.
This defeat infuriated those who had been protesting against the country's increasingly unaffordable housing market all week.
"We are demanding a fundamental right: decent housing, stability and conditions allowing us to construct a decent life project," another protester in Madrid, aged 31, told the AFP news agency.
Spanish media reported that Sanchez might call a snap election for November after the legislation failed to pass, adding that the government would be watching Saturday's protests closely before making a decision.
Sanchez's office declined to comment on the reports.

articles.title: Yemen launches major military operation against Houthis
articles.description: Yemen's internationally recognized government announced a new military offensive to retake Houthi-held territory after rebels cut a key road linking the city of Taiz with Aden.
articles.body:
Yemen's internationally recognized government announced a new military offensive to retake Houthi-held territory after rebels cut a key road linking the city of Taiz with Aden.
https://p.dw.com/p/5Nkh9 The recent Houthi advance followed days of heavy fighting in and around the besieged city of Taiz [September 22, 2014] Image: Mohammed Hamoud/Anadolu Agency/picture alliance Advertisement Yemen's Saudi-backed government on Sunday announced a new military operation to retake territory held by Iran-backed Houthi rebels , as fighting intensified around the key southwestern city of Taiz.
"Today, I announce the start of military operations to retake the remaining territory of the republic and extend the authority of the state and its institutions across the entire national territory," Yemeni Presidential Council chief Rashad al-Alimi said in a televised address.
The announcement came after Houthi fighters captured a key road linking Taiz with the government-held city of Aden, effectively isolating Taiz. The rebels have besieged Taiz for more than a decade.
More than 70 people were reportedly killed in fighting around Taiz over the past day, according to AFP news agency.
The latest developments come amid an escalation between the Houthis and the internationally recognized government in Yemen that is supported by Saudi Arabia, reviving Yemen's civil war after a four-year ceasefire.
A 2022 truce between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia collapsed in July after the rebels allowed an Iranian plane to land in Yemen's capital Sanaa, which defied the Saudis' control over Yemeni airspace.
As a result of the escalation, the Houthis announced a maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia.
Last month, the Houthis seized Yemen's Red Sea coast and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait — a vital global shipping route — from government hands, even as Al-Alimi called for support from the international community.
The Houthis have controlled Sanaa and much of Yemen's more populous western areas since the start of Yemen's civil war in 2014.

articles.title: Hundreds of French schools closed amid protests
articles.description: The student protests that rocked France last week have prompted authorities to keep up to 500 schools closed on Monday. More protests are planned for Tuesday.
articles.body:
The student protests that rocked France last week have prompted authorities to keep up to 500 schools closed on Monday. More protests are planned for Tuesday.
https://p.dw.com/p/5Nkg4 The school protests have spread nationwide, as here in Lyon Image: Laurent Cipriani/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement Several hundred schools in France will close totally or partially on Monday amid security fears following a wave of nationwide student protests, the education minister has said.
The protests by pupils complaining of poor conditions began at one Paris school on September 17 but last week mutated into sometimes violent demonstrations across the nation.
France students protest school conditions To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Education Minister Edouard Geffray said on Sunday that lessons would be totally or partly suspended" in some "400-500" high schools on Monday, as the security conditions "have not been fulfilled."
According to Geffray, the schools were being closed mainly as a precaution, with more large protests planned for Tuesday.
Geffray said the number of schools remaining closed on Monday would be similar to that on Friday but that there was planned to be a "partial, progressive return to lessons."
He said 24 schools had been "burned or ransacked" and 78 education staff members injured since the protests began.
"There are activists — particularly from the far left — who have infiltrated the high school student movement, hijacked it from the students themselves, and engaged in extreme violence," Geffray said.
"Clearly, this poses a risk to both our staff and our students," he added.
Valerie Pecresse, the president of the Ile-de-France region surrounding the capital, said that more than a third of the 468 schools in the region would be shut on Monday.
The protesting teenagers at French high schools, called lycees, have complained of high rates of absenteeism by teachers, school days that are too long and dilapidated facilities.
They have also protested at the lack of adequate cooling on hot summer days, with some towns seeing temperatures of 40 degrees Celsius (104 Fahrenheit) last summer in a country without widespread air conditioning.
Organizers have called for the protests to continue on Tuesday, saying the government was still failing to propose "concrete measures" to remedy the situation.
On Sunday, Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu urged local authorities to make it a priority to fill gaps left by long-term absences and unfilled posts.
He also called a meeting for Tuesday with regional presidents to discuss renovating school buildings that are often in poor condition.
The protests have been marked by several violent incidents, with security forces sometimes using tear gas and batons to disperse the young protesters.
More than 5,000 people, 85% of them minors, have been arrested since the start of the movement.
On Sunday, a 16-year-old was detained after a 59-year-old teacher was hit and doused with gasoline on the sidelines of a protest in the southern town of La Ciotat.
Last week, a group of young people was filmed beating and kicking a policeman on the ground in the eastern town of Belfort.
The French branch of rights group Amnesty International last week described the action taken by police as "disproportionate."
Interior Minister Laurent Nunez has, however, defended security forces, saying they were "not cracking down on young people" but rather "protecting" school and university students wishing to "peacefully voice their demands."

articles.title: Middle East oil exports recover to pre-Iran war levels despite Hormuz attacks
articles.description: Gulf crude exports returned to pre-war levels in September, with producers increasingly relying on alternative routes and ship-to-ship transfers to bypass Hormuz. Iranian exports remain below the pre-war average.
articles.body:
Gulf crude exports returned to pre-war levels in September, with producers increasingly relying on alternative routes and ship-to-ship transfers to bypass Hormuz. Iranian exports remain below the pre-war average.
https://p.dw.com/p/5NkgS Before the Iran war started, the Strait of Hormuz accounted for some 20% of the world’s daily crude oil and LNG supply [FILE: July 21, 2019] Image: Morteza Akhoundi/ISNA/Photoshot/picture alliance Advertisement Middle East crude oil exports , excluding Iran, rose back above pre-war levels in late September despite continued attacks on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz, according shipping data from trade intelligence firm Kpler .
Exports exceeded the pre-war average of about 18 million barrels per day (bpd) on four days in the final week of September, reaching 19.5 million to 22.5 million bpd, according to the data and analytics platform.
When the Strait of Hormuz closed following the start of the Iran war, the seven-day average non-Iranian crude leaving the region fell by 72% in 10 days, Kpler said.
The recovery has relied on alternative routes and ship-to-ship transfers.
In September, about 40% of crude left the Gulf without crossing Hormuz, compared with only 17% before the Iran war .
According to Kpler, more than 70% of the crude changed tankers offshore in the Gulf of Oman in August. In comparison, almost no Gulf crude changed tankers in the Gulf of Oman before the war.
Additionally, Saudi Arabia also increased exports through the Red Sea, while the UAE used its pipeline to Fujairah.
The primary exporters of crude oil in the region were:
Iran, however, remains the major exception, with its exports still well below the pre-war average, primarily due to US policies.
Meanwhile, attacks on vessels have continued around Hormuz. At least seven incidents have been reported in recent weeks.
On October 1, a tanker, Kazimah III, was reportedly struck by an unknown projectile, according to maritime intelligence firm Marisks. All crew members were evacuated safely.

articles.title: US: FBI arrests woman accused of spying on Taiwan's president's family for China
articles.description: A California woman was arrested at Los Angeles International Airport, just before departing for China, with the US officials accusing her of spying on Taiwan's president's son.
articles.body:
A California woman was arrested at Los Angeles International Airport, just before departing for China, with the US officials accusing her of spying on Taiwan's president's son.
https://p.dw.com/p/5NkT3 Wanying Z., who was arrested by the FBI, was also known as Heather Image: via REUTERS Advertisement US officials announced on Sunday that a woman had been arrested by the FBI and accused of spying for China in the United States.
Wanying Z., 34, of Irvine, California, was detained at at Los Angeles International Airport ahead of a scheduled flight to China.
She faces charges of acting as an unregistered foreign agent.
The woman "traveled to Seattle in 2025 and, at the direction of (People's Republic of China) officials, surveilled a close relative of a Taiwanese government official, sending photos, videos and license plate information to those officials," First Assistant United States Attorney Bill Essayli said in an online post.
He added that Z. "coordinated the trip with an associate and used tradecraft to avoid detection."
The woman is due to appear before a Los Angeles federal court on Monday, Essayli wrote.
The FBI said Z. was spying on a son of Taiwanese President Lai Ching-te . While the US agency did not provide the target's name, they later shared a New York Post report identifying him as Lai Ting-yu, who is reportedly a US resident.
In an X post, FBI Director Kash Patel celebrated the arrest, warning foreign adversaries that "America is no longer a safe place to run your espionage operations."
"Allegedly surveil a foreign leader's family on US soil for the PRC — and try to catch a flight back to Shanghai? Not happening," Patel added.
Lai and his Democratic Progressive Party advocate for Taiwan 's distinct identity from China. Their statements often irritate Beijing, which considers the island Chinese territory.
While Washington does not have formal diplomatic relations with Taiwan, the United States is the island's most important international supporter and supplier of weapons .

articles.title: US pulls bombers out of UK's Fairford airbase after arrests
articles.description: Following a suspected terrorist plot targeting the UK's Fairford airbase, the US Air Force withdrew all its B-1 planes from the site.
articles.body:
Following a suspected terrorist plot targeting the UK's Fairford airbase, the US Air Force withdrew all its B-1 planes from the site.
https://p.dw.com/p/5NkR9 US B-1 bombers stationed at RAF Fairford were used for strikes against Iran Image: Alastair Grant/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement A week after several men were detained at the Royal Air Force (RAF) base in the UK's Fairford on suspicion of planning terrorist attacks, a Pentagon official announced that the United States had removed its B-1 bombers from the base northwest of London.
On Sunday, aircraft monitoring sites showed the B-1 aircraft flying out of the UK base.
"While operational security precluded us from ​confirming the movement of our assets and forces ​in real-time, ‌we can acknowledge now that all US bombers that were deployed to RAF Fairford have re-deployed to their home ‌stations in the United States," a Pentagon spokesman wrote ‌in ​a statement.
A dozen B-1 bombers had been stationed at RAF Fairford, the British airbase used by the US. London previously allowed the Pentagon to fly sorties out of Fairford against Iranian missile sites which were threatening ships in the Strait of Hormuz.
UK releases air base plot suspects To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Last Sunday, police were called to a base in southwest England after a local farmer reported a group of men in several vans engaging in "suspicious" activity.
Investigators blocked off the area and called in the bomb disposal teams. However, no explosives were found in the vehicles. Later, the five British nationals arrested in connection to the incident were released on bail .
US President Donald Trump voiced his disappointment over their release.
On Wednesday, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said that Britain had "strong indications" that Iran was involved in a suspected plot targeting the base.
Iran dismissed the accusations as baseless and summoned the British ambassador in Tehran to discuss the issue.

articles.title: Brazil election: Flavio Bolsonaro and Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva head to runoff after tight race
articles.description: Populist Flavio Bolsonaro has secured a thin lead over incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, but the next president of Brazil will be decided in the runoff round, according to the country’s electoral court.
articles.body:
Populist Flavio Bolsonaro has secured a thin lead over incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, but the next president of Brazil will be decided in the runoff round, according to the country’s electoral court.
https://p.dw.com/p/5NiO9 The early count in the Brazilian presidential election puts Flavio Bolsonaro (left) ahead of Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva Image: Alexandre Meneghini/Pilar Olivares/REUTERS Advertisement With votes being counted in Brazil following the presidential election on Sunday, populist Senator Flavio Bolsonaro was leading the race ahead of leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva. Bolsonaro seeks to continue the right-wing populist movement started by his father, Jair Bolsonaro, while Lula is seeking his fourth non-consecutive term.
With more than 99% of the ballots processed, Flavio Bolsonaro has received 47.2% of the vote, and Lula has 45%. Since neither candidate received enough votes to win outright on Sunday, the country's electoral court announced that Bolsonaro and Lula will face each other in a runoff on October 25.
Commenting on the outcome, Bolsonaro said he was "very happy with the real possibility that, three weeks from now, Brazil will give a definitive answer by choosing a modern government."
In turn, Lula said it was "unexpected" as he was convinced he would "win in the first round."
"Tomorrow we start a new campaign," the 80-year-old said. "I am very good in the knockout stage."
In 2022, Lula beat Jair Bolsonaro by only 1.8 percentage points.
You can relive the Brazil election with the recording of our livestream below.
Fabio de Sa e Silva, a professor of Brazilian studies at the University of Oklahoma, told DW that the right was currently on the rise in Brazil.
"The big news is not that we have a runoff... but it is a takeover that happened in Congress by the far-right," the researcher said.
He added that it will be very hard for Lula to govern with Brazil's new Congress, even if he eventually secures another term.
Along with voting for president, Brazil's 160 million registered voters also chose other lawmakers, governors, and some senators.
Those races brought more victories for the Bolsonaro family, with former first lady Michelle Bolsonaro and another son of the former president, Carlos Bolsonaro, both winning Senate seats.
Overall, Bolsonaro's right-wing camp won by far the most Senate seats and will form the largest bloc in the chamber.
Lula and Bolsonaro wrapped up their campaigns on Saturday in Brazil's economic powerhouse state of Sao Paulo.
The 80-year-old Lula capped off his campaign with a tour through the city of Sao Paulo, vowing to "defeat the far right ."
Lula has campaigned on continuing his left-leaning Workers' Party platform, comprising welfare programs, state-funded development and income redistribution.
"The people will have to choose between strengthening the democratic regime and barbarism ... between progress and backwardness," he said as he cast his ballot on Sunday.
Flavio Bolsonaro, 45, has served as the Liberal Party's senator for Rio de Janeiro since 2019. On Saturday, he led a motorcycle parade through Sao Paulo's countryside cities of Santa Barbara d'Oeste and Americana.
He also held up a portrait of his father, while the crowd shouted "mito" — a Portuguese word for "legend" that Jair Bolsonaro's supporters use to refer to him.
The right-wing Bolsonaro has campaigned on hardline security policies and tax cuts, emphasizing high cost of living under Lula, who he has slammed as "incompetent."
"Brazil needs change," the son of the former president said as he cast his vote. "Brazil cannot bear any more suffering, such as high taxes, so many women killed."
The elder Bolsonaro is currently serving a 27-year sentence in prison for attempting a coup to overturn his loss to Lula in the 2022 presidential election. Flavio Bolsonaro has vowed to pardon his father if elected.
Lula's team has cast the Bolsonaro movement as a threat to Brazil's sovereignty, pointing to Flavio and Jair's ties with US President Donald Trump , who last year slapped a 50% tariff on Brazilian imports in response to Jair Bolsonaro's coup trial. The US president called the case a "witch hunt."
Brazilians vote in high-stakes presidential election To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
The younger Bolsonaro has said in interviews he is "more moderate" than his father, who he has nevertheless said will remain "my compass, my point of reference."
Policies where both Bolsonaros are similar include relaxed gun control laws and skepticism of human-caused climate change.
Trump has not endorsed the senator, but has said he is watching the election "very closely."
Brazil finds itself politically divided, and campaigning has been bitter, with online operations from both sides seizing on every gaffe, accusation and rumor, quickly producing slick videos or AI-generated images for social media.
In September, it was revealed Bolsonaro is under investigation for alleged corruption, money laundering and tax evasion tied to the financing of a biopic about his father. He has denied any misconduct.

articles.title: Anthropic report: Is Russia using AI for disinformation in the Central African Republic and elsewhere?
articles.description: An Anthropic report says the AI model Claude was used in pro-Russian campaigns in the Central African Republic. Similar allegations were raised for the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Kenya, Sudan and Mali.
articles.body:
An Anthropic report says the AI model Claude was used in pro-Russian campaigns in the Central African Republic. Similar allegations were raised for the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Kenya, Sudan and Mali.
https://p.dw.com/p/5NTaF The Claude app was allegedly misused by Russian agents Image: Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto/picture alliance Advertisement In Bangui, the capital of the Central African Republic , Russian agents are said to have deliberately used the AI assistant Claude to promote pro-Russian influence. A report titled " Detecting and Countering Misuse of AI ," published by US-based company Anthropic in September, detailed how opposition politicians were monitored, propaganda content was created and disinformation campaigns were supported.
The report claimed that Claude was used primarily to produce content broadcast by Radio Lengo Songo, a radio station that, according to the international investigative collective All Eyes on Wagner, is funded by Russia. The collective, made up of journalists, academics and experts, investigates the activities of the Russian mercenary group Wagner Group and its successor structures, such as the Africa Corps, around the world.
The Anthropic report said the content was pro-Russian and portrayed the Central African government and the Africa Corps mercenaries in a positive light, while taking a critical stance on France and the opposition.
Lou Osborn, a member of All Eyes on Wagner, was involved in the research for the latest report. He believes these methods are part of a practice that has already been observed in connection with the Wagner Group in the Central African Republic. "There have been several arrests of people who were not necessarily closely affiliated with the Touadera regime," he told DW. "They’ve been doing this for several years now." Faustin-Archange Touadera has been president of the Central African Republic since 2016.
"The arrests were the subject of online campaigns in newspapers and on the radio which portrayed those individuals either as proxies for France or Western intelligence services, or as people preparing a coup against Touadera," Osborn added.
Anthropic also reported that Claude was prompted to portray opposition figures as armed militants in an effort to provoke security forces into taking action against them. Anthropic says Claude refused the request. However, the report did not name the opposition figures who were monitored, specify the exact nature of the data collected, or say who received it.
For the opposition, the Anthropic report underscored the determination of the government in Bangui and its Russian allies to get rid of them. Martin Ziguele, chairman of the Movement for the Liberation of the Central African People, referred to an earlier case. "We have been observing this since 2020, when the CPC, a coalition of rebel groups, attacked Bangui. Strangely enough, several media outlets did everything in their power to establish alleged links between certain opposition leaders and the CPC," Ziguele told DW. "There were also attacks against the opposition claiming that we were being paid by foreign countries. There was an attempt to pass a law stating that foreign agents were present in the country. All of this relates to the activities of the Wagner Group, as does this latest revelation."
DW also sought a statement from Russia. "Yes, I heard about [the report] in the news," said Dmitri Sytyi, a representative of the Russian mission in the Central African Republic. "But there are no concrete facts in it. [...] These are vague allegations, without precision and without evidence."
Russia firmly denies the allegations, but the report indicates that the Central African Republic was not an isolated case. According to the report, the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), Kenya , Sudan and Mali were also affected.
In the DRC, Anthropic identified 318 articles that, according to the report, were published by a network of about 70 fake news sites and subsequently distributed by more than 250 fictitious accounts on X. The content supported the positions of the Congolese government against the backdrop of the conflict with Rwanda.
In Kenya, Claude was allegedly used to generate batches of 50 messages at a time that supported the government and were hostile toward the opposition.
In Sudan, Anthropic says AI was used as part of an operation attributed to individuals in the United Arab Emirates — particularly to create fabricated witness statements for the United Nations.
In Mali, meanwhile, an adviser with ties to intelligence services allegedly used Claude to develop a platform for monitoring telecommunications. According to the report, it was designed to target 25 million SIM cards and circumvent the requirement to obtain judicial authorization.
Anthropic says it uncovered and shut down all of these different operations between December 2025 and August 2026, primarily by deleting the accounts involved and strengthening its detection systems.
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: Latvia election: Pro-Ukraine PM Kulbergs set to retain power after historic victory for his party
articles.description: Latvia's prime minister, Andris Kulbergs, looks set to retain power after his party appeared to score the country's biggest election victory since independence.
articles.body:
Latvia's prime minister, Andris Kulbergs, looks set to retain power after his party appeared to score the country's biggest election victory since independence.
https://p.dw.com/p/5Ngfd Centrist Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs (right) is on track for a strong win in the elections Image: Wojtek Radwanski/AFP Advertisement Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs appeared set to remain in power on Sunday after his centrist United List secured 35.3% of the vote in the country's parliamentary election.
The result gives United List 42 of 100 seats and puts Kulbergs in a strong position to form another pro-Ukraine coalition.
With 97% of ballots counted, United List had secured the country's biggest parliamentary election victory since Latvia regained independence from the Soviet Union in 1991.
The party could secure a parliamentary majority with either the nationalist National Alliance or the left-leaning Progressives, political scientist Roberts Kits said.
Kulbergs, a 47-year-old businessman and amateur rally driver, only came to power in May after the previous coalition collapsed over its handling of incidents involving stray Ukrainian military drones.
Latvia vote shaped by Russia fears To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
An exit poll put the the populist Latvia First party in second place with 11.3% — nearly double its share at the last election in 2022. It had courted the country's substantial ethnic Russian minority.
Kulbergs said on Saturday night that he would not cooperate with any pro-Russian parties and specifically ruled out forming a coaltition with Latvia First.
Some 1.5 million people were eligible to vote in the country's 11th parliamentary election since independence in 1991.
The election, which saw 100 seats in the Saeima being contested by 14 parties using a proportional system, was dominated by rising living costs and national security concerns in the small Baltic country which borders both Russia and Belarus .
Russia's ongoing invasion of Ukraine is seen as a direct threat to national security in Latvia which, like Ukraine, is a former Soviet state with a sizeable ethnic Russian and Russian-speaking minority.
Unlike Ukraine , however, Latvia is a member of both the European Union and NATO .
Riga is one of Kyiv's closest partners and supporters, having committed itself by law to spending at least 5% of GDP on defense – leaving less room for spending elsewhere.
Many Latvians complain of high prices and low wages, the economy is sluggish, the health system is under strain, and emigration and an ageing population remain persistent challenges.
Populist movements such as the Sovereign Power/Young Latvians Alliance and the Latvia First party have attempted to exploit discontent by taking a less stringent line towards Moscow and arguing that a complete economic decoupling from Russia is damaging.
Lessons from Latvia: How to deal with Russian hybrid threats To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Nevertheless, no parties proposed any major deviation from Latvia's clear foreign policy alignment with the EU and NATO.
Indeed, four German Eurofighter jets were deployed to protect Latvian airspace during the election in response to a request from Riga.

articles.title: Pakistan and Afghanistan used to be allies but they're edging towards all-out war
articles.description: For years, Pakistan supported the Taliban in Afghanistan. But now Pakistan is bombing its neighbor. How the former allies became adversaries and why negotiations keep failing.
articles.body:
For years, Pakistan supported the Taliban in Afghanistan. But now Pakistan is bombing its neighbor. How the former allies became adversaries and why negotiations keep failing.
https://p.dw.com/p/5Nhw3 Taliban security forces after a Pakistani airstrike in Khost, September 2026 Image: AFP Advertisement On Thursday night, Pakistan attacked targets in Afghanistan . The results of that attack are disputed. The Taliban, the Islamic fundamentalist nationalist movement that controls Afghanistan, says that between nine and 10 civilians were killed, including women and children. But Pakistan claims the strike killed 22 militants and destroyed weapons and ammunition depots.
These early October attacks are just the latest escalation in a conflict between the two countries that reignited mid-September, after months of comparative calm.
The conflict was sparked again after a series of attacks on Pakistani security forces . On September 18, an attack on a police compound in the northwestern city of Kohat resulted in the d eaths of 31 people and more than 100 injured. A splinter group belonging to the Pakistani Taliban, also known as Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan, or TTP, claimed responsibility for the attack in Kohat, in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, bordering Afghanistan.
Pakistan accused Afghanistan of providing the TTP with a safe haven. Afghanistan denies this but clashes at the border and then airstrikes by Pakistan followed.
The TTP in Pakistan is not the same as Afghanistan's Taliban. Although it does have close ideological and personnel ties to the Afghan Taliban, it is an independent organization that fights the Pakistani state.
Many of its fighters sided with the Taliban during that country's long-running insurgency against international and US troops. This is why, after the Taliban returned to power in 2021, the TTP gained more room and more leverage. This has meant that Afghanistan — a former ally of Pakistan — has increasingly become a threat to its neighbor.
Pakistan has asked the Taliban to take action against the TTP, but the close connection between the two make this difficult.
"Because of these personal connections and networks, it is extremely difficult for the Afghan Taliban to break away," says Conrad Schetter, director of the Bonn International Center for Conflict Studies, or BICC.
How 5 years of Taliban rule have changed Afghanistan To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
The connections don't mean that the Taliban has any control over the TTP. There are certainly historical connections between the two, but Schetter doesn't believe that equals any sort of strong, direct influence.
"The Taliban are simply not prepared to take orders from Islamabad," adds Thomas Ruttig, co-director of the Afghanistan Analysts Network, a think tank working between Kabul and Berlin. "They won't let anyone outside interfere."
This means the Pakistani policy of supporting the Taliban in order to gain influence in Afghanistan hasn't worked.
There's also another older conflict that has an impact on the current situation. This involves what is known as the Durand Line, drawn in 1893 by a British diplomat and an Afghan emir to mark spheres of influence between British India and Afghanistan.
The current border between Afghanistan and Pakistan follows the Durand Line and also divides an area on both sides, homeland to Pashtuns, who make up the largest ethnic group in Afghanistan and second largest in Pakistan.
So the border dispute here isn't just about territory, it's also about identity.
"Ethnic and nationalist elements play a significant role in the conflict," Schetter tells DW. Many Pashtuns still refuse to accept the border that the Durand Line created.
In Pakistan, the country's long-running rivalry with India also plays a part. A friendly Afghanistan would have been advantageous for Pakistan. But India has also strengthened its ties to the Taliban.
"While Islamabad once viewed Afghanistan as a source of 'strategic depth' in its rivalry with India, it now increasingly views its north-western neighbor as a liability," an analysis by British think tank Chatham House notes.
Pakistan still has power over Afghanistan, though. As a landlocked country, Afghanistan relies on trade routes through neighboring countries, and Pakistan in particular. Pakistan can use border closures and trade restrictions to exert pressure even as the Taliban regime is trying to reduce dependence on Pakistan and find new economic and political partners.
Trade and security considerations are now becoming tangled. Pakistan has held talks with the TTP that were mediated by the Taliban and ceasefires were agreed upon . Talks between Pakistan and Afghanistan also took place. But none of the temporary agreements resolved the crucial question of how to prevent attacks on Pakistan from Afghan territory.
So in parallel with diplomacy, Pakistan has also been relying on economic and political pressure, for example, by closing borders and restricting trade and by sending Afghan refugees back into Afghanistan.
An analysis by the US-based Council on Foreign Relations notes that the Taliban are worried that if they crack down on the TTP too hard, they will drive the group towards another extremist militant group, the Islamic State in Khorasan Province or IS-K. This group opposes the Taliban.
The conflict recently escalated to another level. At the end of September, Kabul reported 28 killed and 32 captured fighters who had infiltrated Afghanistan from Nuristan province, Pakistan. The Taliban accused Pakistan of supporting its armed opponents, something Pakistan has denied.
"It is known from past decades that Pakistan has regularly supported armed groups on the Afghan side — for example, the Mujahideen during the Soviet occupation and later the Taliban," Ruttig points out. "What's new though is that Pakistan apparently also supports parts of today's armed anti-Taliban opposition."

articles.title: In Tigray, Ethiopian government forces have advanced against a northern rebel group, reports indicate
articles.description: Reports indicate Ethiopian government forces have made advances against a northern rebel group. Renewed fighting has raised fears the conflict could spill over into the wider region.
articles.body:
Reports indicate Ethiopian government forces have made advances against a northern rebel group. Renewed fighting has raised fears the conflict could spill over into the wider region.
https://p.dw.com/p/5NiWS Rebel groups had seized control of airports and sections of Tigray's capital on September 23 Image: AFP Advertisement Government forces in Ethiopia said they have recaptured an airport in Tigray's capital that was seized by rebel groups last week, in the northern region's worst outbreak of violence since a bloody civil war ended in 2022.
Several news agencies cited anonymous government sources on Saturday as saying Ethiopian federal forces now control Alula Aba Nega Airport in Mekelle.
"The military is in full control of the airport. That much I can confirm," an Ethiopian general told the Associated Press on condition of anonymity.
The AFP news agency, citing a "humanitarian source," reported rebel groups were leaving the city as Ethiopian government forces moved in.
Neither side has issued an official statement on the status of who controls Mekelle, and reporting is complicated by communication blackouts and restricted media access.
Pulling out of Tigray's capital would be a setback for the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) , which recently aligned with several other armed opposition groups in northern Ethiopia.
The new rebel alliance transforming the Tigray conflict To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
The TPLF has been the dominant force in Tigray since ousting a government-appointed administration earlier this year, and then appointing former wartime regional leader Debretsion Gebremichael as regional president.
The Addis Ababa-based government's Ethiopian National Defense Force has been fighting off a renewed rebel offensive since late September.
The TPLF seized the airport in Mekelle on September 23, along with launching attacks on government positions in the neighboring regions of Afar and Amhara, initially having made gains before being pushed back this week.
Gebremichael issued a statement on Thursday, promising to continue guerrilla attacks on government forces, similar to what took place when rebels lost control of Mekelle in 2020.
The TPLF, which ruled Ethiopia from 1991 to 2018, seeks to topple Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government. More than 600,000 people were killed in a civil war from 2020 to 2022.
The renewed unrest in northern Ethiopia has led to tensions spilling across the region , with fears of wider regional conflict in the Horn of Africa.
For years, Ethiopia has accused its northern neighbor Eritrea of providing support to Tigray rebels, alongside Sudan and Egypt. All three countries deny this.
Last week, Ethiopia and Eritrea cut diplomatic ties , with both countries expelling diplomats and closing embassies.
The African Union said it was concerned by the growing tensions between Ethiopia, Eritrea and Egypt, and has called on all sides to show maximum restraint.
Eritrea accuses landlocked Ethiopia of planning to invade and seize access to the Red Sea
The TPLF's Debretsion said in his video message that "the war is regional and it is a war to control the Red Sea."
